summary: Sets out requirements for NATs that handle DCCP so applications like streaming can work consistently. They are similar to the existing requirements for NATs handling TCP. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: A NAT is like a mail clerk who rewrites return addresses. This tells the clerk exactly how to handle one type of parcel, so replies find their way home.

questions: what are the nat requirements for dccp
how long should a nat keep dccp sessions
why does dccp not work through nat
subtitle: Thirteen rules that tell NATs how to carry DCCP connections so applications keep working.

tldr.problem: NAT devices are not typically capable of handling Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) traffic, so DCCP applications such as streaming often cannot work through them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out requirements REQ-1 to REQ-13 for NATs that choose to handle DCCP. They cover mapping, filtering, timeouts, checksums and Service Codes, and are modelled closely on the earlier TCP requirements.
tldr.outcome: A NAT that meets the requirements greatly increases the likelihood that DCCP applications work. NATs that do not handle DCCP are simply outside its scope.

today: RFC 5597 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 150), and no RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why DCCP Needs NAT Rules
sections.content:
This is a Best Current Practice document. It applies only to NAT devices that want to handle DCCP (defined in RFC 4340). Most deployed NATs are not expected to handle it and are not the target. All definitions and requirements of RFC 4787 are inherited, and the structure and much of the content follow RFC 5382, the TCP requirements.

A NAT must rewrite the DCCP source port on outgoing packets, the destination port on incoming packets, and the DCCP checksum to compensate for address and port changes. Changing the IP addresses normally invalidates the checksum, so DCCP cannot pass a NAT that only rewrites the IP header, as some generic transport-protocol support does.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk has to change the address on the outside and fix the check number inside. A clerk who only changes the outer address breaks the parcel.

sections.title: Starting and Keeping Connections
sections.content:
REQ-1 says a NAT MUST use endpoint-independent mapping for DCCP. REQ-2 says it MUST support all valid DCCP packet sequences for connections started from either side. That includes the 3-way handshake and the simultaneous-open mode of RFC 5596, which adds the DCCP-Listen packet. If both endpoints are behind NATs, the normal asymmetric DCCP connection does not work and a simultaneous-open must be used.

For externally initiated connections, REQ-3 recommends endpoint-independent filtering when application transparency matters most, or address-dependent filtering when stricter filtering matters most. REQ-4 says a NAT MUST wait at least 6 seconds after an unsolicited inbound DCCP-Listen or DCCP-Sync before answering with an ICMP error or a DCCP-Reset. If the NAT translates an outbound DCCP-Request in that time, it MUST silently drop the original packet.

REQ-5 covers idle sessions. A NAT that times out sessions MUST default to an established connection idle-timeout of 124 minutes or longer and a transitory connection idle-timeout of 4 minutes or longer.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk must handle parcels from either side, wait a few seconds before saying no to a stranger, and keep a waiting parcel for a good long while before giving up on it.

sections.title: Other Requirements for DCCP
sections.content:
Several requirements repeat rules from RFC 4787 and RFC 5508 that affect DCCP, without relaxing them. REQ-7 forbids port overloading. REQ-8 requires hairpinning, of type external source IP address and port. REQ-9 says a NAT SHOULD translate ICMP Destination Unreachable messages, and REQ-10 says no ICMP message may terminate the mapping or connection it refers to.

REQ-6 differs from TCP: any Application-Level Gateways in a NAT MUST NOT affect DCCP. The RFC explains that DCCP is loss tolerant, which makes payload changes hard to track, and that no DCCP-capable gateways were known when it was written.
sections.plainLanguage: A few more rules: do not mix up two senders on the same door number, let two people in the same building reach each other, and never close a parcel's route just because a warning note came back.

sections.title: Checksums and Service Codes
sections.content:
DCCP supports partial checksum coverage, so the Checksum Coverage field says how much of a packet the checksum protects. REQ-11 says a NAT that translates a packet with a valid checksum MUST make the translated checksum valid. If it recalculates the value, it must honor the coverage as described in Section 9.2 of RFC 4340. REQ-12 says a NAT MUST NOT modify the Checksum Coverage value, since that would violate the receiver's integrity assumptions.

REQ-13 says a NAT MUST NOT modify the DCCP Service Code, a 4-byte value naming the application-level service. Further guidance on Service Codes and middleboxes is in RFC 5595.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk must keep the check number correct after changing the address, and must not touch the label saying what kind of service the parcel is for.

sections.title: Security and the UDP Fallback
sections.content:
The security concerns of RFC 4787 apply here. The RFC says REQ-1 and REQ-6 through REQ-13 introduce no new known security concerns, and neither does REQ-2. The delayed ICMP error in REQ-4 may reveal the presence of a NAT to an attacker, while silently dropping the packet makes problems harder to diagnose and forces applications to wait through several retransmissions. Implementers must weigh these effects.

For REQ-5, a NAT may actively probe whether a connection is alive, or an administrator may configure more conservative timeouts, to guard against state exhaustion attacks. Separately, if a NAT cannot be updated to support DCCP, DCCP can be encapsulated in UDP, which most NATs already handle. The RFC treats that as out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Answering strangers can reveal that the clerk is there, and staying silent makes problems harder to spot. If the clerk cannot learn the new rules, parcels can be repacked in a box the clerk already knows.
